title: Values and ranges in Go
summary: Use a typed slice, a range loop, and a condition to count positive values.

scenario.briefing: The campus API receives stock changes as a slice of integers. Count the positive changes in Go.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.

hints: The range loop already visits every value.
Increment count inside the if body.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a declared int is uninitialized.
misconceptions.feedback: Go gives every value a zero value. count starts at 0 without an explicit assignment.

misconceptions.description: Trying to mutate the slice element through the range value.
misconceptions.testDescription: The range loop counts only positive values.
misconceptions.feedback: Range yields a copy of each element. Use the index when a mutation is required.

misconceptions.description: Believing a nil slice cannot be ranged over.
misconceptions.feedback: A nil slice has length zero. Ranging over it is safe and runs the body zero times.

sections.title: Go values and decisions
sections.body: Go declares values with var count int = 3 or the short form count := 3. Types are checked at compile time. Integers, floats, strings, and booleans are distinct types. Every type has a zero value, such as 0 or an empty string. An if statement can include a short initialization before the condition. Go has one loop keyword: for. It can act as a counting loop or a range loop over a slice.

steps.title: Check the semantics

statements.label: A slice carries a pointer, a length, and a capacity.
An int variable starts at an undefined value.
A range loop over a slice yields the index and a copy of the value.
A nil slice cannot be ranged over safely.

steps.explanation: Go initializes values to their zero value. Range yields the index and a copy; the length is part of the slice descriptor.
hints: An int starts at zero, not an undefined value.
A nil slice has length zero and can be ranged over.
